variants.name: Traits class template with a primary mapping and specializations
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical form: a class template with no data members whose members are the associated types, constants and static functions for one type or family; the primary template reads them from the type's own nested members, full and partial specializations supply them for types that cannot be edited (raw pointers, fundamental types, arrays), and the algorithm names typename traits<T>::member instead of the type's members. A default template argument (class traits = char_traits<charT>) lets a user substitute a different description - a case-insensitive comparison - without changing the algorithm, and <type_traits>, std::iterator_traits, std::char_traits and std::numeric_limits are the standard-library instances. Still the right shape when the descriptor must carry associated types or values; prefer a concept when you only need to constrain or select behaviour.
pitfalls: Every dependent member needs typename/template disambiguation, and a missing nested member in the primary template produces an error inside the library template rather than at the call site.
A specialization must be reachable where the trait is instantiated: one declared after the point of use, or in the wrong namespace, is silently ignored and the primary template is used instead.
An empty primary template plus explicit specializations is the safe default - a 'helpful' primary template that guesses values for unknown types compiles and then misbehaves.

variants.name: Detection idiom over std::void_t (C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: Here the property is computed rather than declared: a partial specialization over std::void_t<decltype(...)> inherits from std::false_type when the probed expression is ill-formed and from std::true_type when it is well-formed, giving traits such as has_push_back that synthesise a description from the type's shape; the detector wrapper generalises it (detected_or_t, is_detected from Library Fundamentals TS v2). Choose it when you must support C++11/14/17 toolchains, when the trait has to be a boolean usable in enable_if, or when probing an expression is exactly the question being asked; prefer C++20 concepts in new code because they express the same requirement with diagnostics that name the failure.
pitfalls: SFINAE only covers the immediate context: an ill-formed nested construct (a bad member inside a class template) is a hard error, not a substitution failure, so a probe that looks negative can fail the whole build.
A typo in the probed expression is indistinguishable from 'not supported' and silently reports false; keep a positive case in the test suite (a type that really does provide the member).
Detection traits report syntax, not semantics: has_push_back is true for a type whose push_back has the wrong signature or returns nonsense, so the trait does not replace the requirement's contract.

variants.name: Named concepts and requires-clauses (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: A named concept is a compile-time predicate over a type that replaces the boolean trait: template <class T> concept Serializable = requires(const T& t, std::ostream& os) { { t.serialize(os) } -> std::same_as<void>; }; and then void log(Serializable auto const& v). Concepts take part in overload resolution through subsumption - the more constrained overload wins without enable_if layers - and violations are reported as the unsatisfied concept instead of a substitution backtrace, so the trait machinery is no longer needed to constrain or select behaviour; the descriptor survives exactly where the payload is data (iterator_traits, numeric_limits).
pitfalls: A concept satisfied by a syntactic match is not a semantic guarantee; cppreference gives Addable-style checks that accept an operator+ which is not addition.
Subsumption is structural: two separately written concepts with identical bodies do not subsume each other, so an overload set ranked by such 'equivalent' concepts is ambiguous.
Concepts cannot be specialised or explicitly instantiated, so a concept cannot be extended for a new type from outside the way a traits specialization can - the descriptor still owns that role.
